paper.title: Robust Harmful Features Under Jailbreak Attacks: Mechanistic Evidence from Attention Head Specialization in Large Language Models

read: full text (arXiv HTML): Sections 1, 3-6 and Appendices A (overlap distributions, threshold and bandwidth sensitivity), B (exclusion of MLP and LayerNorm), D (detector design, hyperparameters, training-free baselines, over-refusal, attribution), E (Llama-3-70B); C (qualitative examples) skimmed

claims.claim: Successful jailbreaks of a safety-tuned language model work by suppressing a small set of early-layer attention heads that normally feed the model's refusal signal, rather than by erasing the model's representation of harmful intent, and it is the attack's template tokens, not the harmful request itself, that suppress them. Supported only if, on two safety-tuned chat models, heads identified from successful attack pairs as carrying less of the refusal direction under attack are causally sufficient: pushing just 8 of them against the refusal direction on requests the model normally refuses raises attack success from about 0% to at least 80%, all of them to at least 80%, while the same number of random heads gives at most 15%; and if token-level attribution shows the attack-template tokens pushing these heads strongly negative (median at or below -1 standard deviation) while pushing the other attack-sensitive group positive, with the harmful-request tokens affecting both groups alike (medians within 0.2).
claims.decision_rule: Llama-3-8B and Llama-2-7B: ASR at k=8 ACHs >= 80% and all ACHs >= 80%; random heads <= 15%; template-token contribution median <= -1 (ACH) vs >= +1 (SAH); harmful-token medians within +-0.2.

claims.claim: Because a jailbroken model still represents the harmful intent internally, reading those internal signals detects harmful prompts, including adversarially wrapped ones, far better than the model's own refusals and about as well as trained guard classifiers, without any training. Supported only if ablating the mid-layer heads that stay active under attack lowers mid-layer refusal-direction activation under attack by at least 10% in both analysed models; and if a training-free detector that averages standardised refusal-direction projections from the most harmful-vs-benign-separating components improves the sample-weighted macro-F1 over ten balanced moderation and jailbreak benchmarks above the model's own refusal behaviour by at least 0.08 on each of seven open models from three families, reaches at least 0.80 on all three adversarial benchmarks for at least six of the seven, has its best model above the best trained guard model, and beats gradient-based and steering-based training-free detectors while flagging fewer hard benign prompts than the model's own refusals.
claims.decision_rule: SAH ablation Mean|Act| drop >= 10% (both models); W.Avg F1 Ours - Vanilla >= 0.08 on 7/7 models; adversarial sets (HB-A, SAL, WJB) >= 0.80 on >= 6/7; best Ours W.Avg > WildGuard 0.880; Ours > GradientCuff and CAST (Qwen-7B); OR-Bench hard specificity > Vanilla.

experiments.text: Find the heads. Setup: Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Llama-2-7B-Chat; refusal direction by difference in means at the end-of-instruction position (layer 12 and 14); back-project it through each head's OV circuit (ignoring LayerNorm and MLPs) to get a head-specific direction, and score each head by its output's projection on that direction. Data: Alpaca benign prompts; harmful requests from public benchmarks that the model refuses; attacked variants (GCG, AutoDAN, many-shot, PAIR) that succeed, paired one-to-one; of about 10,000 attack samples only 176 (Llama-3) and 378 (Llama-2) pairs qualify. Two-stage KDE overlap filter (threshold 0.5): heads separating harmful from benign, then among them heads whose harmful and attack distributions differ, split by direction into attack-suppressed (ACH) and attack-strengthened (SAH). Result: Llama-3 has 80 stable harmful-salient heads, 21 ACHs, 17 SAHs (416 heads in layers 0-12); Llama-2 43, 20, 19 (480 heads in layers 0-14); over 60% of ACHs lie in layers 0-3 and SAHs in layers 5-12.

Intervene on the suppressed heads. Setup: on refused harmful inputs (baseline attack success about 0%), subtract the head's refusal-aligned component (strength 0.8) at an increasing number of ACHs; control with the same number of random heads, 10 seeds, 95% intervals. Result: attack success reaches 95.0% (Llama-3) and 81.6% (Llama-2) at 8 heads, following an S-shaped curve, and 99.5 +- 0.3% and 83.7 +- 1.1% with all ACHs, against 4.0 +- 3.7% and 10.2 +- 11.6% for random heads. Generations stay coherent and on-topic (qualitative); no capability benchmark is run, and the authors note this shows a sufficient pathway, not the one real attacks necessarily use.

Attribute head activations to input tokens. Setup: split each head's standardised contribution, using attention weights from the end-of-instruction position, into the part from the original harmful-request tokens and the part from attack-template tokens. Result: on harmful-request tokens ACHs and SAHs have similar contributions (medians within +-0.15); on template tokens ACHs are pushed to a median of about -1.5 and SAHs to about +1.5, a separation above three standard deviations, in both models.

Check sensitivity of the head classification. Setup: vary the overlap threshold from 0.1 to 0.9 (same for both stages) and the KDE bandwidth scale from 0.2 to 2.0. Result: ACH / SAH counts for Llama-3 go 0 / 0 at 0.1, 7 / 8 at 0.4, 21 / 17 at 0.5, 45 / 51 at 0.6 and 207 / 207 at 0.9, so the sets depend strongly on the threshold (the authors report conclusions holding for 0.4-0.6); bandwidth changes keep the head ranking (Spearman >= 0.93 for Llama-3, >= 0.98 for Llama-2) but strong under-smoothing reshuffles the sets (Jaccard 0.15-0.18 at scale 0.2, 0.7-0.9 from 0.6-0.8).

Repeat the classification at larger scale. Setup: Llama-3-70B-Instruct, refusal direction at layer 26, 1,728 heads in layers 0-26; only 40 successful pairs from the same 10,000-sample attack pool (under 0.5%). Result: 200 harmful-salient heads, 62 ACHs in layers 0-6 and 83 SAHs in layers 8-20, with the same early-suppression and mid-layer-persistence heatmap pattern; no interventions at this scale.

Ablate the heads that stay active. Setup: apply the same suppression to SAHs on successful attack inputs and measure mean absolute refusal-direction activation across mid-layer heads (Llama-2 layers 14-25, Llama-3 12-25). Result: Llama-2 drops from 0.222 to 0.181 (18%) and Llama-3 from 0.0062 to 0.0053 (14%), against 0.397 and 0.0086 under the original harmful inputs, so attack inputs already carry much less than harmful inputs and SAHs account for part of what remains.

Define the detector and benchmark. Setup: at the end-of-instruction position, project every head's output onto the refusal direction, standardise by benign statistics, keep components whose harmful-vs-benign KDE overlap is below 0.3, average the top m standardised scores and flag the input above a threshold chosen per model on a validation set to maximise F1 (m and threshold vary widely: e.g. Gemma-2-9B m = 577 of 635, Gemma-2-27B m = 38 of 952). One forward pass, white-box access needed. Ten 1:1-balanced benchmarks from the safety-eval framework: WildGuardTest, ToxicChat, OpenAI Moderation, Aegis 1 and 2, SimpleSafetyTests, HarmBench-Vanilla, and adversarial WildJailbreak, SALAD-Bench, HarmBench-Adversarial; macro-F1 and its sample-weighted mean. Baselines: each model's own refusal behaviour and trained guard models (LlamaGuard3 and 4, Qwen3Guard, WildGuard).

Compare detection across seven models. Result: weighted macro-F1, refusal behaviour vs detector: Gemma-2-2B 0.470 vs 0.853, Gemma-2-9B 0.514 vs 0.816, Gemma-2-27B 0.519 vs 0.798, Llama-2-7B 0.664 vs 0.752, Llama-3-8B 0.797 vs 0.888, Qwen-7B 0.506 vs 0.860, Qwen-14B 0.470 vs 0.847; guards 0.599 (LlamaGuard3), 0.666 (LlamaGuard4), 0.877 (Qwen3Guard), 0.880 (WildGuard). On SALAD-Bench the detector reaches 0.94-0.99 except Llama-2 (0.649), where refusal gives 0.27-0.89; on WildJailbreak 0.84-0.94. ToxicChat and OpenAI Moderation stay weaker (0.44-0.80 and 0.65-0.76), below WildGuard and Qwen3Guard on several models.

Compare with other training-free detectors and check over-refusal. Setup: on Qwen-7B, GradientCuff (gradients of a refusal loss) and conditional activation steering (CAST); on Llama-3-8B, OR-Bench-Hard-1K of hard benign prompts. Result: weighted macro-F1 0.856 against 0.741 and 0.611 (CAST is better on WildJailbreak, 0.945 vs 0.923); on OR-Bench, F1 / hard specificity 0.606 / 0.418 against 0.571 / 0.329 for refusal behaviour, 0.510 / 0.053 for GradientCuff and 0.453 / 0.290 for CAST, so the detector still flags most hard benign prompts.

Note what favours the detector in the comparison. Setup: the detector's threshold and top-m are tuned per model on a validation set to maximise F1, the refusal baseline is the model's unmodified behaviour, and the guard models are used off the shelf; component selection reuses harmful and benign prompt sets that overlap in source with some benchmarks. The detector also requires white-box activations, so it is not a drop-in replacement for a guard model.

dropped: Justification for excluding MLP and LayerNorm (argument, no new experiment); qualitative ablation generations; detector token-attribution visualisation.
notes: Drafted from scratch from arXiv HTML for the dataset50 rebuild, without consulting earlier claims or references. References kept at the level of model internals; no attack prompts reproduced. c1 smallest gain over refusal: Llama-2 0.752 - 0.664 = 0.088; adversarial >= 0.80 fails only for Llama-2 (SAL 0.649, HB-A 0.797). The prompt-source overlap in the confound is my inference from the shared benchmark families (HarmBench, AdvBench-style sets), not stated by the authors.
